To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) TransE, TransH, TransR and DistMult are state-of-the-art embedding models for link prediction; (ii) the best model depends on the dataset; (iii) the performance of all embedding models is limited by sparsity in the data.

(1) TransE is the state-of-the-art model for knowledge base completion on FB15k, FB13 and FB15k-23, (2) TransE is also the state-of-the art model for knowledge base completions on WN18 and WN18RR, (3) TransR outperforms TransE on FB13 and WN18RR and TransR outperformed TransE on WN18, and (4) TransR outperform all other models on FB15

(1) TransE and TransH are the best performing models for FB15k, FB13, WN11 and WN18, (2) TransE, DistMult, TransH and TransR are the best models for FB15K-237, and (3) TransE and DistMult are the best models in WN18RR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two main tasks.
the following questions: (1) How to represent entities and relations? (2) How to represent knowledge bases? (3) How to perform knowledge base completions?

the following questions: What are embedding models of entities? What is the state of the art in knowledge base completion using embedding models? How do different types of embedding models compare to each other? How do different embedding model variants compare to each other within the same embedding model family?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TransE is still the best model, but that the performance of other models is getting very close to TransE.

the TransE model is the current state-of-the-art model for link prediction, but that the TransE and DistMult models perform similarly, and that the DistMult model is more interpretable and easier to train.

the TransE and ComplEx models are currently the best performing models on the FB15k and WN18 datasets, and that the TransE, ComplEx, and RotatE models are the best performing models for the FB15k-2-37 and WN18RR datasets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the state-of-the-art models are able to achieve an F1 score of 0.7 or above, and a mean reciprocal ranking of below 50 on the standard datasets.
, while the state-of-the-art is still far from perfect, there are many exciting directions to pursue, and we expect that knowledge base completion will continue to be an active area of research.

the state-of-the-art is currently achieved by a combination of the following techniques: a) use of a multi-task learning objective, b) using a neural architecture that includes both a convolutional component and a recurrent component, c) using an entity representation with a separate vector for each entity, d) using a relation representation that is a vector of the same size as the entity vectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is no one-size-fits-all embedding model, but that there are many different approaches that can be used to achieve state-of-the-art performance, with some approaches working better on some tasks and others working better on other tasks.
, while the performance of embedding models is improving rapidly and the best performing models are now approaching human performance, there is still room for improvement.

the best-performing models on these datasets are based on a combination of entity embeddings, relation embeddings, and entity-relation embeddings, and that these models are typically trained by minimizing the sum of a loss based on negative sampling and a loss based on triple scoring.
